 Live .  14,743 viewing 14743 viewing Live page Updated 2 minutes ago Trump and Putin shake hands as Xi welcomes leaders to summit in China
 Summary
 China's Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin are pictured together in Shenzhen for the first time - images show the leaders shaking hands 
 They're in China for the Apec summit. Earlier, Xi welcomed Trump with a hug on the tarmac - a carefully choreographed moment of flattery, writes our correspondent 
 The pair will have historic trilateral talks with Putin on Thursday - Xi earlier called the Russian leader an "old friend"
 Our Russia editor says some newspapers are already calling this visit a "diplomatic victory" for Putin - simply because it's happening 
 Meanwhile, Trump arrives from the Philippines where he attended another summit - here's a recap of the trip so far

 Live Reporting
 Edited by Manish Pandey, with Laura Bicker, Steve Rosenberg and Stephen McDonell in China and Nada Tawfik travelling with President Trump
 Russian media hail 'historic handshake' as Moscow positions itself as equal to US and China published at 12:21 GMT 12:21 GMT 
 Liza Fokht 
BBC News Russian 
 Russian media are describing the meeting between Xi, Putin and Trump in Shenzhen (which we have just seen) as "the main images of the day". One state news agency called the scene a "historic handshake".
 This is precisely the image the Kremlin was hoping for.
 Unlike the US and China, Russia is not among the world's three largest economies. Yet at the Apec summit, Vladimir Putin clearly feels like a leader equal to Xi and Trump.
 Moscow is sending a message to the world: attempts to isolate Russia have failed, despite its ongoing war in Ukraine.
 And while tomorrow's meeting between the leaders is unlikely to produce any practical results, Putin has already achieved his main objective. 
 His very presence in this club, and the attention of the world's media, allows Moscow to position itself as one of the world's unshakable powers.

 Trump accompanied by key allies with 'different views' on China published at 12:17 GMT 12:17 GMT 
 James FitzGerald 
North America reporter 
 This visit to China by US President Donald Trump comes as his top team wrestle with how to handle China in the wake of a recent alleged spying scandal that has engulfed American tech firm Nvidia. 
 It has unfolded against the backdrop of a fierce AI race - in which the US and China are the world's top two competitors. Nvidia is central to Trump's mission to dominate in the field. 
 The president himself has acknowledged that he has competing voices in his ear when it comes to dealing Beijing.
 Last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of US-made chips - a key part of AI tech. 
 Both men have accompanied Trump for his visit to Asia. Asked about the two men's relationship before setting off, Trump responded: "They're fine. They have two different views."
 He added: "One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blow-up with China."
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Howard Lutnick (left) and Scott Bessent (centre) have differing views
 The US administration has taken relatively tough steps over the issue in recent days, indicating that the figures who take a hawkish stance to China are proving influential.
 For one, the US has confirmed it is investigating a Singapore-based company which is suspected of breaking US restrictions by helping Nvidia's chips to China.
 The Trump administration also renewed its efforts to further curb China's access to advanced semiconductors - which are also critical for the AI industry.

 Apec family photo released published at 12:13 GMT 12:13 GMT 
 We've just received the "family photo" of the leaders of economies in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec).
 Front and centre is China's President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan. US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are also in the front row - with Trump next to Xi.
 Other leaders, including Canada's Mark Carney and Japan's Sanae Takaichi are in the second row.
 Image source, Reuters

 Criticism over US sanctions unites China and Russia published at 12:09 GMT 12:09 GMT 
 Jack Lau 
Global China Unit, reporting from Hong Kong 
 Image source, Reuters President Xi Jinping may have given President Donald Trump a rare personal welcome at Shenzhen airport, but he joins President Vladimir Putin in sharply criticising US economic sanctions and restrictions.
 At the Apec CEO summit this morning, Xi called for "free and open trade", while Putin touted Russia's resilience under sanctions.
 Russia's military, technology and industrial sectors have been targeted over Moscow's war in Ukraine. China, meanwhile, faces sanctions and restrictions linked to human rights, advanced technology and military development.
 Xi has repeatedly criticised sanctions from Washington DC, here at Apec and elsewhere. Beijing says it does not recognise unilateral sanctions imposed outside the UN Security Council, where China and Russia both hold veto powers.
 Dr Wan Qingsong, a Russia expert in Shanghai, says both countries are facing growing pressures as supply chains fragment and governments move to protect domestic industries, particularly hi-tech sectors.
 "For China and Russia, working more closely together is not only about mutual economic benefit - it is also a way to guard against global economic risks," says Wan, also the deputy director of East China Normal University's Russia Studies Centre.

 Trump has been relishing the warm receptions on this trip published at 12:04 GMT 12:04 GMT 
 Nada Tawfik 
North America correspondent, travelling with President Trump 
 This has been a fast-paced trip to Asia for the US President. 
 It’s clear from his various engagements that he’s been relishing the warm reception he’s received from Manila to Shenzhen. 
 At nearly every stop, the red carpet has been laid out and world leaders have gone to great lengths to make him feel special, even if privately they are thinking about what the US might look like in two years - when he’s no longer president.
 That includes President Xi, who as we mentioned personally greeted him on the tarmac in Shenzhen. 
 While much is being made of the unprecedented summit between Presidents Trump, Xi and Putin, even US officials have tried to manage expectations. 
 Trump wants a new, modernised arms pact that includes China along with Russia. 
 US officials say the trilateral meeting is a first conversation and a moment for China, which has a much smaller arsenal compared to the US and Russia, to "step up to the adults table on a matter on international importance".
 China will be carefully managing the trilateral, to make sure it’s a symbolic moment for all three leaders, but also that it doesn’t overshadow their summit.

 Trump, Putin and Xi seen together for the first time published at 11:47 GMT 11:47 GMT 
 Laura Gozzi 
Europe reporter 
 Image source, Reuters Some more now on the interaction between Trump, Putin and Xi. 
 Russia's Kremlin pool team has posted a video on Telegram showing Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump together on a red carpet ahead of tonight's gala dinner in Shenzhen. 
 In the video, Trump, Xi and Xi's wife are standing next to each other when Putin approaches. 
 Trump and Putin - who haven't met since the Russia-US summit in Alaska in August 2025 - seem to greet each other warmly, shaking hands first and exchanging pats on the shoulder.
 It's the first time Xi, Trump and Putin will have a trilateral summit.
 The three leaders are due to meet tomorrow afternoon.

 Carney does his own outreach in Asia as US trade deal remains elusive published at 11:38 GMT 11:38 GMT 
 Nadine Yousif 
Reporting from Toronto, Canada 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in China earlier this week
 Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has already been in Asia for several days ahead of the Apec summit, where he announced a free trade deal with the Philippines and held a bilateral meeting with China's Xi Jinping. 
 It's all part of his broader push to reduce Canada's reliance on the US as the country still grapples with Donald Trump's tariffs on its key sectors.
 US tariffs have since led Carney to break away from American trade policies vis-a-vis China.
 Earlier this year, Canada significantly reduced tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), allowing up to 49,000 in the country. The US, meanwhile, still tariffs Chinese EVs at 100%. 
 Ahead of his meeting with Xi, Carney suggested that China's automotive industry could help replace a gap in Canada's sector if a trade deal with the US is not reached.
 Afterwards, China and Canada agreed to further tariff relief on pork and seafood, as well as certain steel and aluminium products.
 Neither mentioned vehicles, but Ottawa said Chinese EVs are expected to soon enter the Canadian market. 
 Closer integration on auto manufacturing with China, however, still depends on where trade talks with the US land.
 Negotiations are ongoing and progress has been made but some key differences remain, Carney said this week.
 Many in Canada will be watching to see how Carney and Trump interact at Apec.

 Trump meeting with Canadian and Mexican leaders - White House published at 11:25 GMT 11:25 GMT 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum next to her Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco Alvarez
 President Trump is separately meeting with both Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney today in China, the White House says.
 All three leaders are attending summit in Shenzhen and they are all members of the Apec group.

 What has already happened and what else are we expecting? published at 11:10 GMT 11:10 GMT 
 Malu Cursino 
Live reporter 
 Image source, Reuters US President Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen for a rare trilateral meeting between him, Vladimir Putin and the host, Xi Jinping.
 The red carpet was rolled out as Trump's Air Force One landed in Shenzhen, with President Xi greeting him on the tarmac - what China correspondent Laura Bicker describes as a "carefully choreographed diplomatic moment" .
 Quoted by Chinese state-run news agency Xinhua, President Xi has voiced his desire for a "constructive, strategically stable relationship" with Washington.
 Several hours before Trump's arrival, Russian leader President Putin landed in Shenzhen, with Putin and Xi holding talks, and the Russian leader saying the foreign policy strategy of the two countries was working.
 Trump in Manila 
 Trump's Shenzhen arrival follows a 21-hour stay in Manila for the Asean Summit, where he met India's Narendra Modi, Japan's Sanae Takaichi and Australia's Anthony Albanese. 
 While in the Philippines, Trump signed trade agreements with Thailand and the Philippines - but both are light on details and specific commitments.
 At a dinner with South East Asia leaders, the US president said: "This is one of the world's most vibrant and productive regions filled with the tremendous potential."
 Filipino President Ferdinand Marcos Jr hosted Trump at the Malacañang presidential palace and sent Jollibee fried chicken to the US president's party as a midnight snack.
 What's to come? 
 Trilateral talks between Moscow, Beijing and Washington will be Thursday's focus. Issues relating to global peace will be high on the agenda, according to China's foreign ministry.

 Chinese state media: Trump thanks Xi for warm welcome to Shenzhen published at 10:35 GMT 10:35 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images A Chinese state-run news agency describes the welcome given to US President Donald Trump as warm, with a salute from the military honour guard, children presenting flowers and fighter jets above.
 Xinhua quotes Xi as saying that when he visited the US in September, Trump and his wife made a "special trip to the airport" to welcome them and held a "grand welcoming ceremony". 
 "I welcome your renewed visit to China and look forward to in-depth exchanges of views with you on major issues concerning China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the global order, and to promote the development of a constructive strategic and stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and equality," the agency quotes Xi as saying. 
 It adds that Trump thanked Xi for coming to the airport to personally welcome him.

 Putin and Trump 'will meet a few times' at summit - Kremlin senior aide published at 10:21 GMT 10:21 GMT 
 Laura Gozzi 
Europe reporter 
 Image source, Getty Images Kremlin senior aide Yury Ushakov has said Putin and Trump - who are due to meet Xi Jinping on Thursday - could meet at tonight's gala dinner.
 "And they will definitely meet tomorrow," Ushakov adds in comments to Russian state TV. "Both during the plenary session of the Apec summit and immediately after it concludes."
 "The leaders will meet, believe me, and they will have a substantive conversation, regardless of where they happen to be sitting - in armchairs, on chairs or on stools - or standing face-to-face, looking each other in the eye. The meeting will take place. Our president and the US president will meet a few times over the course of the summit," Ushakov says.
 He also hints the meeting could take place on the sidelines of the summit, without the presence of large delegations.

 Historic Xi-Trump-Putin meeting reportedly to take place at a villa published at 10:12 GMT 10:12 GMT 
 BBC Chinese 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images The trilateral meeting between China, the US and Russia is reportedly set to take place at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen on Thursday, with security significantly tightened ahead of the talks.
 The state-owned compound, which opened in 1997, has long hosted Chinese leaders and high-profile foreign visitors to the city.
 Beijing’s decision to opt for a more private setting rather than a formal conference venue suggests the meeting is “more of a sideline rather than a separate, significant summit on its own”, says Minseon Ku of DePaul University, a specialist in summit diplomacy.
 “Xi would want that, since, as the host of Apec, China would want the Apec summit to be the primary event and would not want the trilateral meeting to overshadow it,” she tells the BBC.
 Professor Shaoyu Yuan of New York University, who studies US-China diplomacy, notes that Kylin Villa is relatively easy to secure. Its proximity to the airport would also allow Trump to depart directly after the meeting.
 "The setting carries less diplomatic formality than an official venue in Beijing, framing the roughly one-hour meeting as a working-level engagement. The lower the ceremonial profile, the lower the political cost if the meeting produces no tangible outcomes," he says.

 Nvidia spy scandal looming over Trump and Xi meeting published at 09:57 GMT 09:57 GMT 
 Laura Bicker 
China correspondent 
 Image source, AFP via Getty Images Jensen Huang is out as CEO of Nvidia, but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
 The allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with businesswoman Alice Huang - who US officials suspect of being a Chinese spy - are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
 Beijing's foreign ministry described the spy claims as a "smear against China", and Chinese officials worry this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.
 Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms accessing advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. Beijing has called the new rules "economic coercion". 
 The Nvidia scandal may spiral into something bigger for US-China ties.

 Taiwan demands participation on 'equal basis' published at 09:40 GMT 09:40 GMT 
 Benny Lu 
BBC Chinese 
 Apec is one of the few international bodies of which Taiwan is a formal member – the self-governed island is in fact a founding member – and its attendance at the leaders' summit usually goes fairly smoothly. 
 This year's gathering in China, however, has introduced complications because of tensions with Beijing. 
 China says it welcomes Taiwan's participation under the "one-China principle", which asserts that Taiwan is not an independent territory but a part of China. But Taipei has rejected this, with President William Lai saying last week that Taiwan's participation should be regarded on an "equal basis".
 "Apec is different because Taiwan already enjoys formal membership," Felix Brender, a postdoctoral fellow in Taiwan studies at Harvard, says, arguing that it'll be hard for Beijing to challenge Taipei's participation – unlike in the cases of the UN and the World Health Organisation, where Taiwan is not officially recognised.

 Takaichi arrived in Shenzhen earlier amid frosty Japan-China ties published at 09:29 GMT 09:29 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also arrived in Shenzhen a little earlier.
 This is Takaichi's first official visit to China since taking office in October 2025 - and comes as relations between the two countries have fallen to the lowest point in over a decade.
 A row erupted between Tokyo and Beijing in November last year, when Takaichi appeared to suggest that Japan could activate its self-defence force in the event of an attack on Taiwan, a self-governed island which China claims as its own.
 This set off a war of words, then led to trade and export restrictions.
 Analysts believe formal talks between Takaichi and Xi on the sidelines of Apec are unlikely, although they may have a brief exchange such as a handshake.

 This is no ordinary welcome published at 09:24 GMT 09:24 GMT 
 Laura Bicker 
Reporting from Shenzhen 
 This isn’t simply an airport greeting by Chinese President Xi Jinping. This is a carefully choreographed diplomatic moment.
 Xi understands the value of this gesture, as it is thought to be the first time that he has greeted a foreign leader at the airport as President.
 Firstly, he is mirroring Trump’s own actions. 
 The US president was there to meet Xi at the airport in Washington earlier this year - and now the Chinese leader is returning the compliment.
 But Xi will also be aware that Trump places considerable importance on personal recognition, ceremony and status. 
 By not delegating this task, the Chinese president is flattering his US counterpart and making him feel important by singling him out for the honour of a personal greeting.
 Xi may hope that this sign of good will smooth the path for negotiations over trade, Taiwan and technology. 
 He can also afford to be gracious here without losing face. China is already controlling the setting and arrangement for the unprecedented summit between Trump, Xi and Putin.
